Simplex weights minimising a V-weighted predictor discrepancy

Source: R/fit_scm.R
sc_weights_simplex.Rd

Solves the synthetic-control weight problem exactly: $$\min_w (Z_1 - Z_0' w)' V (Z_1 - Z_0' w) + \lambda \sum_j w_j (Z_1 - Z_{0j})' V (Z_1 - Z_{0j})$$ over the unit simplex (w >= 0, sum(w) = 1), where V = diag(v) and lambda is the Abadie-L'Hour penalty (zero by default, the classic synthetic control).

Usage

sc_weights_simplex(Z0, Z1, v = rep(1, ncol(Z0)), penalty = 0)

Arguments

Z0

Donors x predictors matrix, already standardised.

Z1

The treated unit's predictor vector.

v

Non-negative predictor weights (the diagonal of V).

penalty

The Abadie-L'Hour penalty lambda, non-negative. The scale is that of the standardised predictors. See fit_scm() for when to use it.

Value

A numeric vector of donor weights, non-negative and summing to 1.

Method

A primal active-set method – Lawson and Hanson's non-negative least squares algorithm, adapted to the simplex. It keeps a working set of donors, solves the equality-constrained problem on that set exactly (through a pseudo-inverse, so a singular set is handled), steps back to feasibility when a weight would turn negative, and adds the donor whose gradient most violates optimality. It stops at the exact KKT point: every donor with positive weight has the same gradient and no donor has a lower one. Starting from the nearest donor, it typically needs about two steps per donor in the final support.

Two alternatives were tried and rejected. A first-order (Frank-Wolfe) solve needs over 12,000 iterations on the highly collinear pre-period outcomes of the Proposition 99 panel, and at any practical iteration cap returns weights well short of the optimum. A dual QP solver needs a ridge to make the singular quadratic term invertible, which with a penalty makes the problem nearly linear and the solve numerically unreliable.

Uniqueness

When the treated unit lies inside the donors' convex hull, many weight vectors can fit the predictors equally well, and they imply different counterfactuals. Which of them is returned then depends on the order in which donors enter the working set – deterministic, but arbitrary. fit_scm() warns when the fit is exact. A positive penalty makes the solution unique (Abadie and L'Hour 2021).

References

Lawson, C. L. and Hanson, R. J. (1974). Solving Least Squares Problems. Prentice-Hall, chapter 23.

Examples

Z0 <- matrix(c(0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2), nrow = 3)
sc_weights_simplex(Z0, c(1, 1), v = c(1, 1))
#> [1] 0 1 0
